title: Section check: Museums, heritage and connections
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 16–20. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Seeing the clay piece in a building would give it a different context. What is context?

options.text: The material that an object is made of
options.feedback: Not quite. The clay is the material. Context is the things around an object that help explain it. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: The person who gave it to a museum
options.feedback: Not quite. A donor is one part of an object's history. Context is everything around it that helps explain it. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: The things around it that explain it
options.feedback: Yes. Its place, light, labels and nearby works all change how we see an object.

questions.question: A museum label names the donor who gave an object. What does the donor's name show?

options.text: One part of the object's history
options.feedback: Yes. A donor's name is one part of the object's provenance. Records can still have gaps.

options.text: Every owner back to the first maker
options.feedback: Not quite. One name does not prove the whole chain of owners. Records may have gaps. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: Who made the object a long time ago
options.feedback: Not quite. The donor gave the object to the museum. The makers of these two works are not recorded. Look back at Lesson 16.

questions.question: The mosque's walls are tangible heritage. What does tangible mean here?

options.text: Skills that people pass on to others
options.feedback: Not quite. Skills that people pass on are intangible heritage. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Things you can see and touch
options.feedback: Yes. The walls are real things you can touch. The skills of the builders are a different kind of heritage.

options.text: A report about repairs to a building
options.feedback: Not quite. A report is a source about a building. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Look back at Lesson 17.

questions.question: Why does the Great Mosque of Djenné need people's work every year?

options.text: It must be painted a new colour.
options.feedback: Not quite. The mosque is made of earth. Every year, people put new mud plaster on it. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Its earth walls need new plaster.
options.feedback: Yes. Its sun-baked earth bricks are covered in mud plaster. People put on new plaster every year.

options.text: It is built again from new each year.
options.feedback: Not quite. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. The yearly work is new plaster. Look back at Lesson 17.

questions.question: The Vietnamese plate and the Chinese jug both have blue designs. Which claim would need more evidence?

options.text: One maker copied the other
options.feedback: Yes. Looking alike does not prove copying. We would need other evidence for that.

options.text: Both have blue painted designs
options.feedback: Not quite. You can see the blue designs in the photos. Copying is what would need more evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.

options.text: Their shapes are not the same
options.feedback: Not quite. You can see the plate and the jug have different shapes. Copying would need more evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.

stimulus.title: A made-up potter
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Ama is a potter in the made-up town of Sela. She sees a flower design on a bowl from far away. She uses it on her own plates. She adds local fruit to it and changes the shape to suit her buyers.

questions.question: Which word from Lesson 18 describes what Ama does?

options.text: Export
options.feedback: Not quite. Export means sending goods to another place to sell. Ama changes a design. Look back at Lesson 18.

options.text: Attribution
options.feedback: Not quite. Attribution means naming a work's maker, place or time from evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.

options.text: Adaptation
options.feedback: Yes. Ama changes an idea to fit a new setting and her own buyers. That is adaptation.

questions.question: Posada's skeleton pictures used satire. What is satire?

options.text: Paper with cut-out designs
options.feedback: Not quite. Paper with cut-out designs is papel picado. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: An offering on an altar
options.feedback: Not quite. An offering, or its altar, is an ofrenda. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: Humour that criticises power
options.feedback: Yes. Satire uses humour to make fun of how people act, or of power.

questions.question: In one region of Mexico, the festival is called Xantolo. What does this show?

options.text: One festival name holds many local forms.
options.feedback: Yes. The clothes, music and roles are not the same in each group. One name holds many local stories.

options.text: Every community celebrates in the same way.
options.feedback: Not quite. Place, family and belief shape different forms. Xantolo is one example. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: The festival began with Posada's skeleton print.
options.feedback: Not quite. Posada did not invent the festival. It is much older than his print. Look back at Lesson 19.

stimulus.title: A made-up research question
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Rani wants to know how people look after an old earth building in the made-up town of Kesso. She has three sources. One is a photo of the outside. One is a report on its care, with a date. One is a postcard of it at sunset.

questions.question: Which source best fits Rani's question?

options.text: The photo of the building's outside
options.feedback: Not quite. A photo shows shape and material. It does not explain how the building is looked after. Look back at Lesson 20.

options.text: The dated report on its care
options.feedback: Yes. A report on its care explains how the building is looked after. Choose evidence that fits the question.

options.text: The postcard showing it at sunset
options.feedback: Not quite. A postcard shows a pretty view. It does not explain the care. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.question: The record of the clay piece from Java does not name its building. What should a careful explanation do?

options.text: Leave the missing detail as a question
options.feedback: Yes. The evidence does not settle this. So the missing detail can stay a question.

options.text: Make up a likely name for the old temple
options.feedback: Not quite. An explanation should not use an invented temple name. Look back at Lesson 20.

options.text: Say that it must come from Borobudur
options.feedback: Not quite. The record does not prove that it came from Borobudur. Look back at Lessons 16 and 20.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how museums, care and traditions shape what a work means.
results.middle: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 16–20, then try again whenever you like.
